## Overview
This chronicles the steps taken whilst making a `genoscape` for American Kestrel. The order in which we discuss building up this map is different from the order in which we put layers down to actually make the map. Here, we will start with making the genoscape, which is actually the part that sits atop the whole map.  But we do that because that is the part that will actually change from species to species, and we want everyone to be relatively fresh for understanding those mutable parts.  Once the genoscape is dealt with, we will then talk about the next layer of country and state boundaries, and also coastline polygons.  We do this, because it doesn't take too long to plot these features, and using them is a good way to figure out the desired extent of your map and to decide upon a projection.  Finally, we will talk about the bottom layer of the map, which is the raster with earthforms and shading from Natural Earth Data.

## Packages Needed

### Non-standard Packages

This work draws on a few functions that I have in packages that I have up on GitHub,
namely:

1. **Eric Anderson's fork** of `tess3r`.  Note that you can't use the default version of `tess3r`,
you have to use Eric's fork of it, which has some extra functionality.
2. Eric's package `genoscapeRtools`

Get those packages like this:
```{r, eval=FALSE}
remotes::install_github("eriqande/TESS3_encho_sen")  # for special version of tess3r
remotes::install_github("eriqande/genoscapeRtools")  # for Eric's genoscapeRtools
```

### Standard Packages

The rest of the packages you need can be downloaded from CRAN.  If you don't have
them you should get them: `raster`, `sf`, `fields`, `downloader`, and `tidyverse`. The last one there gets ggplot2
and a number of other packages by Hadley Wickham.

You can get those like this:
```{r, eval=FALSE}
#install.packages(c("raster", "sf", "tidyverse", "fields", "downloader"))
```

### Load the Packages We will work with

```{r, comment=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(raster)  # important to load before tidyverse, otherwise it masks select()
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(ggspatial)
library(scales)
library(terra)
library(tess3r)
library(genoscapeRtools)

```

## Making the genoscape

The genoscape can be thought of as the bright colors smeared across space that show where different
genetically identifiable groups of birds reside on the breeding grounds.  These genoscapes
are stored as rasters, and transparency is used to indicate how much confidence one has
in the genetic identification of individuals in different areas.  These rasters are made
by interpolating Q-values from a program like STRUCTURE or ADMIXTURE between individuals
that were sampled in space. 

### Input Data
Normally you would input the ancestry matrix created in STRUCTURE or ADMIXTURE. But since I've created the genoscape already, I'm just providing you the raster of the genoscape, with the colors and you can plot this for your figures.


#### Breeding Bird Lat-Longs
We also need to know where those individuals were sampled in space. We have that here- though use the file I created specifically for the breeding birds from your previous tutorial.
```{r, message=FALSE}
met<-read_delim("input/Rubias/AMKE_186SNPgenotypes.breeders.412inds_197Radinds.stateFID.hwe.ped.locationfile_fix.txt",delim="\t") %>%
  rename(indiv=Sample_Name)

#Put the meta data in order of the Qmatrices:
LatLong_tibble <-met %>% group_by(State) %>% summarise(meanLat=mean(latitude),meanLong=mean(longitude))

LatLong_tibble
```

#### Breeding Bird Cluster Colors

The Q-values correspond to different clusters, as shown above.  We must specify
the colors that we wish to assign to each of those clusters.  We do that with a named
vector like this:
```{r}
cluster_colors <-  c(
  West = "#ffff33", #west yellow 
  TX = "#ff7f00", #TX, orange 
  East = "#377eb8", #East, blue
  FL = "#984ea3", #FL, purple 
  AK = "#00ffff") #AK, cyan 

show_col(cluster_colors)
```

For fun, we can plot these to see what they look like:
```{r}
enframe(cluster_colors) %>%
  mutate(x = 1:n(),
         y = 1:n()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = name)) +
  geom_point(pch = 21, size = 12) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colors)
```

#### Breeding Bird Shapefile

Finally, we need to have a GIS Shapefile that tells us the range of the breeding
birds, so that genoscape can be clipped properly.  We read this shapefile with the 
`st_read()` function from package `sf`. American Kestrels have a range that goes into South America, where we do not have sampling, so we crop to North America.
```{r, results='hide'}
breeding <- st_read("AMKE_shapefiles_rasters/eBird_range/AMKE.range_smooth.sf.WGS84.Ebird.shp") %>% filter(season=="breeding")
#crop<-c(-152.9703,-37.20669,0,68.98193)
breeding_crop <- st_crop(breeding, c(xmin=-152.9703, xmax=-37.20669, ymin=25.2, ymax=68.98193))

```

For grins, we can plot those polygons to see what they look like.
```{r}
ggplot(breeding_crop) + 
  geom_sf() +
  theme_bw()
```

### Preparing the data for tess3Q_map_rasters
Here is the raster of the AMKE genoscape. Read it in, and name the layers so they match with the color assignment above.
```{r}
genoscape_brick1 <- stack("AMKE_shapefiles_rasters/AMKE_crop.genoscape_brick.tif")
crs(genoscape_brick1) <- "EPSG:4326"
summary(genoscape_brick1)
names(genoscape_brick1) <- c("West", "TX", "East", "FL", "AK")

```

That gives us a raster brick of Q-values associated with each cell in the raster, but
those values are not always constrained between 0 and 1, so we have to massage them 
a little bit in the next section.

### Scaling and cleaning the genoscape_brick

For this we use the function `genoscapeRtools::qprob_rando_raster()`.  This takes the raster
brick that comes out of tess3Q_map_rasters() and does some rescaling and (maybe) some random sampling to return a raster of colors that I hope will do a reliable job of representing (in some way) predicted assignment accuracy over space.
See `?genoscapeRtools::qprob_rando_raster` to learn about the scaling options, etc. (However, I am not convinced that all of those options are reliably estimated.)

This will squash the raster brick down to a single RGBA (i.e., four channels, red, green, blue and alpha) raster brick. You can adjust the alpha (the transparency) by adjusting teh alpha_exp parameter. The higher it is, the more transparency there is.
```{r}
genoscape_rgba <- genoscapeRtools::qprob_rando_raster(
  TRB = genoscape_brick1,
  cols = cluster_colors, 
  alpha_scale = 2, 
  abs_thresh = 0.0, 
  alpha_exp =1.8, 
  alpha_chop_max = 230,
  scale_min_to = 0
)

# at this point, we must be explicit about adding a projection to the raster.
# This adds the info for a regular lat-long projection
crs(genoscape_rgba) <- "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs +ellps=WGS84 +towgs84=0,0,0"
```

We can easily plot this with the function `layer_spatial` from the `ggspatial` package:
```{r}
ggplot() + 
  ggspatial::layer_spatial(genoscape_rgba) + 
  theme_bw() +
  coord_sf()
```

Note that if we wanted to add the actual sampling points to this (that are given
in `long_lat_tibble`), we can use ggspatial's `geom_spatial_point()` function.
/Users/clairelabuda/Downloads/AMKEproject/AMKE.Plate58.Wint.SoutheastUS.rep_indiv_est.inclRES_result.filt_certain.assignment.meta.xlsx
```{r}

#Rub_result<-read_delim("~/Downloads/Supp_Table_2.txt",delim="\t")
Rub_result<-read.xlsx("output/Rubias/AMKE.all.rep_indiv_est.inclRES_US.exclRES_MX_result.incl_meta.Appendix2.xlsx",sheet=1,detectDates =T) %>% filter(Stage!="Breeding")



#write_xlsx(Rub_result, "~/Downloads/Rub_result.xlsx")

Rub_result <- Rub_result %>%
  mutate(
    max_prob = pmax(AK, West, East),
    assignment2 = case_when(
      max_prob < 0.8 ~ "Uncertain",
      AK == max_prob ~ "AK",
      West == max_prob ~ "West",
      East == max_prob ~ "East",
    ) 
  ) 


Rub_certain <- Rub_result %>%
  filter(!is.na(assignment2), assignment2 != "Uncertain")

#write.table(Rub_certain, "genetics_certain1.txt", sep = "\t", row.names = FALSE)

geno_simple<- ggplot() + 
  layer_spatial(genoscape_rgba) + 
  geom_spatial_point(data = LatLong_tibble, mapping = aes(x = meanLong, y = meanLat),shape=1) 
geno_simple

 
map_assignRub_geno <-geno_simple + 
  geom_spatial_point(data = Rub_certain, mapping = aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude,color=assignment2,shape=Stage)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c( "cyan","#377eb8","#ffff33", "purple")) +
theme_bw() +
  coord_sf()

map_assignRub_geno


```

## Coastlines, Countries, States, and Provinces

Since we will be using the Natural Earth Data Set for the raster background of our map, we will also use the Natural Earth lines and polygons.  The Natural Earth data set is
an amazing, open-source resource for making beautiful maps.  Check it out at
[naturalearthdata.com](https://www.naturalearthdata.com/).  


### Plot the Coastlines and estimate where we want to clip

First read it in directly from website:
```{r}
coastlines <-  st_read("/vsizip//vsicurl/https://naciscdn.org/naturalearth/10m/physical/ne_10m_coastline.zip/ne_10m_coastline.shp")
```
Now, let's just crop out the part that we want.  This is somewhat key:
right here we will define the extent in lat-long of the region that
we want to plot... You should match this to the previous tutorial.
```{r}
# note! it is important to put the elements of domain in this
# order, because the function raster::extent() is expecting thing to be in this order, and doesn't parse the names of the vectors
# the way sf::st_crop() does.
sf_use_s2(FALSE)
domain <- c(
  xmin = -180, 
  xmax = -40,
  ymin = -50,
  ymax = 82
)

coast_cropped <- st_crop(coastlines, domain)

```

Then plot the cropped part:
```{r}
ggplot(coast_cropped) + 
  geom_sf() +
  coord_sf()
```

### All the lines, plus the genoscape

OK, that was pretty reasonable.  Now crop all the stae and country lines to `domain` and plot them, and put the genoscape on top of that, too.
```{r}
countries_cropped <- st_read("/vsizip//vsicurl/https://naciscdn.org/naturalearth/10m/cultural/ne_10m_admin_0_countries.zip/ne_10m_admin_0_countries.shp") %>%
  st_crop(domain)
states_cropped    <- st_read("/vsizip//vsicurl/https://naciscdn.org/naturalearth/10m/cultural/ne_10m_admin_1_states_provinces.zip/ne_10m_admin_1_states_provinces.shp") %>%
  st_crop(domain)
```

Now, plot it all.  Notice we do it by just adding layers.
```{r}
mapg <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = coast_cropped) +
  geom_sf(data = countries_cropped, fill = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = states_cropped, fill = NA) +
  ggspatial::layer_spatial(genoscape_rgba) +
  geom_spatial_point(data = LatLong_tibble, mapping = aes(x = meanLong, y = meanLat),shape=1) + 
  theme_bw() 

# now plot it under default lat-long projection
mapg +
  geom_spatial_point(data = Rub_certain, mapping = aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, col=assignment2),size=2)+
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("cyan","#377eb8","#ffff33")) +
  coord_sf(xlim=c(-165,-55),ylim=c(-10,70),expand=F) 

```

That is looking like it should, but the projection is pretty ugly.  In the next section we will consider projection.

## Projecting

The new version of `ggplot2` makes it super easy to project everything on the fly by passing the projection to `coord_sf()`.   For things in North America, it seems that a Lambert conic projection does a nice job of keeping British Columbia and Alaska from looking way too big. We can define such a projection with a string, like this:

```{r}
lamproj <- "+proj=lcc +lat_1=20 +lat_2=60 +lat_0=40 +lon_0=-100 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +ellps=GRS80 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs"
```

Now, let's see how our developing map looks under such a projection.  We just define `lamproj` as 
a coordinate reference system and pass it in to `coord_sf()`:
```{r}
mapg +
  geom_spatial_point(data = Rub_certain, mapping = aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, col=assignment2),size=2)+
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("cyan","#377eb8","#ffff33")) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(lamproj))
```

I would call that decidedly better with the projection.

## The pretty-map background

Now, all that remains is to put all of this on top of a nicely tinted map that shows landforms and things.  Note that once we have such a layer under the rest of this stuff, we will probably omit the coastline layer, since it gets a little dark where the coastline is highly dissected.

### Downloading Natural Earth rasters

I am going to recommend that you get the hypsometrically tinted Natural Earth map with water bodies and rivers on it, and you might as well get the one that has some ocean 
basin coloring too.  We will put it into a directory in the project called `ne_rasters`.  Note, this expands to about half a gig of data. 

```{r}


name <- "HYP_HR_SR_OB_DR"            # or "HYP_HR_SR_W_DR" for full resolution
url  <- sprintf("https://naciscdn.org/naturalearth/10m/raster/%s.zip", name)

options(timeout = 3600)             # large file; the default 60 s will time out
download.file(url, paste0(name, ".zip"), mode = "wb")
unzip(paste0(name, ".zip"), exdir = name)
```
### Read in the raster and crop it

Reading a large raster in with the raster package does not take up much memory, because it leaves it on disk.  So we will open a connection to
the big, massive raster using the `brick` function from the `raster` package
and then crop it:
```{r}

hypso <- rast(file.path(name, paste0(name, ".tif")))
if (crs(hypso) == "") crs(hypso) <- "EPSG:4326"   # georeferenced via .tfw; set CRS if missing
hypso

#hypso <- brick("~/Downloads/AMKEproject/HYP_HR_SR_OB_DR/HYP_HR_SR_OB_DR/HYP_HR_SR_OB_DR.tif")
#hypso_cropped <- crop(hypso, extent(domain)) 

# Crop to exact extent
desired_ext <- ext(-180, -10, -50, 90)
hypso_bg_cropped <- crop(hypso, desired_ext)

# Save
writeRaster(hypso_bg_cropped, "AMKE_shapefiles_rasters/hypso_background_extended.tif", overwrite=TRUE)

```

Now, we just add `hypso_cropped` in with `ggspatial::spatial_layer()` below all of our
other layers (dropping the coastlines), and we might make country and state lines thinner (and different sizes):

Seeing that sort of small on the screen does not really do justice to it.  You can `ggsave` it
in whatever size is desired.  For whatever the final product is going to be, you will
want to mess with the line thickness on those country and state borders...

## Clipping a rectangle out of that

While that looks nice, most people might prefer to have the
background part there in a rectangle, rather than a conic surface.  We can
do that by setting the xlim and ylim to `coord_sf()`.  But, note that
we have to do that in terms of the units that the Lambert projection is referring to,
not just in simple lat-long coordinates (i.e. we have to project those too!)

I've done this already, so easy peasy for you. Let's plot this below. Note it will take a bit!
```{r}
rectangled <- ggplot() +
  ggspatial::layer_spatial(hypso_bg_cropped) +
  geom_sf(data = countries_cropped, fill = NA, size = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = states_cropped, fill = NA, size = 0.1) +
  ggspatial::layer_spatial(genoscape_rgba) +
  geom_spatial_point(data = LatLong_tibble, mapping = aes(x = meanLong, y = meanLat),shape=1) +
#  geom_spatial_point(data = Rub_certain, mapping = aes(x = Long, y = Lat, col=assignment),size=2)+
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("cyan","#377eb8","#ffff33")) +
  geom_spatial_text(data = LatLong_tibble, mapping = aes(x = meanLong-2, y = meanLat+2,label=State),size=3) +
  theme_bw() + 
  coord_sf(
    crs = st_crs(lamproj), 
    xlim = c(-3968118, 3671262), 
    ylim = c(-1699797, 4264362),
    expand = FALSE)  # expand = FALSE means put the axes right at the xlim and ylim

rectangled 

#ggsave("AMKE.genoscape.wbreedingpoints_meanLatLong.clip.rubias_assignment.pdf")
```


Okay, that does it.  In reality, you would probably want to expand the original `domain`
to be a bigger chunk of the earth, so that when you cut stuff off there was more left...


## A final note

If you want to add more elements to the figure you can do so by giving them
a lat-long and making a simple features tibble out of it and then putting them
there using geom_sf().  It all fits nicely
into the ggplot framework.

```{r}
# Load winter bird assignments
winter_birds_gen <- read_delim("output/Rubias/AMKE.all.rep_indiv_est.inclRES_US.exclRES_MX.result.filt_certain_withAssignments01.txt", delim = "\t") %>% filter(Stage!="Breeding") %>% mutate(Sample_type="Genetics")

winter_birds_geo <- read_csv("input/MigConn/AMKEbandingrecoverymatrix_filt.csv") %>% rename(assignment=Cluster,longitude=winter_long,latitude=winter_lat,Sample=band) %>% mutate(Sample_type="Band-Recapture")
# Rename coordinates
winter_birds_gen <- winter_birds_gen %>%
  rename(
    latitude = Latitude,
    longitude = Longitude
  )

winter_birds_gen %>% group_by(assignment) %>% tally()
```

#read in ecoregions
```{r}
ecoregions <- st_read("AMKE_shapefiles_rasters/winter_ecoregion/AMKE.winterEcoregions.simple.sf.WGS84.noWater.Ebird.shp")
ecoregions <- ecoregions %>%
  mutate(node = case_when(
        Region == "Marine West Coast Forests" ~ "MWCF",
            Region == "Northwestern Forested Mountains" ~ "NWFM",
    Region == "Highland/Interior Mexico" ~ "HIM",
    Region == "Highland Central America" ~ "HCA",
    Region == "Northwest Mexico" ~ "NWM",
    Region == "Atlantic Lowland Mexico" ~ "ALM",
    Region == "California" ~ "CAL",
    Region == "Southcentral US" ~ "SCUS",
    Region == "Southeastern US" ~ "SEUS",
    Region== "Southwest Mexico" ~ "SWM",
    Region == "Northern Andes" ~ "NAndes",
        Region == "Eastern Temperate Forests" ~ "ETF",
        Region == "North American Deserts" ~ "NAD",
    TRUE ~ Region
  ))
centroids <- cbind(
  ecoregions,
  st_coordinates(st_centroid(ecoregions))
)

winter_colors <- c(
  "Alaska" = "cyan",
  "West" = "yellow",
  "East" = "dodgerblue",
  "FL" = "#000066"
)


#see where ecoregions overlap with points
winter_sf <- winter_birds_gen %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)

winter_sf <- st_transform(winter_sf, st_crs(ecoregions))

points_with_regions <- st_join(winter_sf, ecoregions, join = st_intersects)

ecoregions_with_points <- ecoregions %>%
  filter(Region %in% unique(points_with_regions$Region))

centroids_filtered <- cbind(
  ecoregions_with_points,
  st_coordinates(st_centroid(ecoregions_with_points))
)

#make plot
winter_map <- ggplot() +
  ggspatial::layer_spatial(hypso_bg_cropped) +
  #geom_sf(data = coast_cropped, fill = NA, size = 0.2) +
  ggspatial::layer_spatial(genoscape_rgba, alpha = 1.1) +
  geom_sf(
    data = ecoregions,
    aes(color = NULL),
    lwd=0.2,
    alpha = 0.4
  ) + #might be size = 0.2 not lwd

  geom_sf(data = countries_cropped, fill = NA, size = 0.15) +

  geom_spatial_point(

    ),

    size = 3
  ) +

  scale_color_manual(values = c("cyan","#377eb8","#ffff33")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(17,16)) +
  
  theme_bw() +

 coord_sf(
    crs = st_crs(lamproj),
    xlim = c(-3568118, 4671262),
    ylim = c(-4799797, 3664362),
    expand = FALSE
  )

winter_map
```

##CREATES PIECHARTS based on ecoregions: too broad
```{r}
# Compute centroids for ecoregions
ecoregion_centroids <- ecoregions %>%
  st_centroid() %>%
  mutate(
    X = st_coordinates(.)[,1],
    Y = st_coordinates(.)[,2]
  ) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(Region, X, Y)

# --- Aggregate birds by ecoregion ---
filt_pies <- winter_birds_gen %>%
    filter(!is.na(longitude), !is.na(latitude)) %>% 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude","latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_join(ecoregions, join = st_within) %>%  # assign each bird to an ecoregion
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(
    AK = sum(assignment == "AK", na.rm = TRUE),
    West = sum(assignment == "West", na.rm = TRUE),
    East = sum(assignment == "East", na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  left_join(ecoregion_centroids, by = "Region")

# --- Plot map with scatterpie ---
# Define your colors for each assignment
pie_colors <- c(
  "AK" = "cyan",
  "West" = "yellow",
  "East" = "#377eb8", 
  "FL"= "purple"
)

# Add scale_fill_manual() to your plot
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = ecoregions, fill = NA, color = "gray50") +
  geom_scatterpie(
    aes(x = X, y = Y, group = Region),
    data = filt_pies,
    cols = c("AK", "West", "East"),
    color = NA,
    alpha = .9,
    pie_scale = 1.6
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pie_colors) +  # <-- colors here
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(4326)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Wintering Bird Assignments by Ecoregion")
```

#Creates piecharts based off of grid
```{r}
# -------------------------------
# Convert birds to sf + project to meters
# -------------------------------
birds_sf <- winter_birds %>%
  #filter(!is.na(longitude), !is.na(latitude)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(5070)   # NAD83 / Conus Albers (good for ecology)

 winter_birds_gen %>% group_by(assignment) %>% tally()
```
 
```{r}
# -------------------------------
# Create 100 km grid covering ALL birds
# -------------------------------
grid_100km <- st_make_grid(
  st_as_sfc(st_bbox(birds_sf)),  # ensures full coverage
  cellsize = 250000,             # 100 km
  square = TRUE
) %>%
  st_sf(grid_id = 1:length(.))

# -------------------------------
# Assign birds to grid cells
# -------------------------------
birds_grid <- st_join(birds_sf, grid_100km, join = st_within)

# -------------------------------
# Summarize assignments per grid cell
# -------------------------------
filt_pies <- birds_grid %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  #filter(!is.na(grid_id)) %>%   # remove any edge cases, can't: AK is on edge in TX
  group_by(grid_id) %>%
summarise(
  Alaska   = sum(assignment == "Alaska",   na.rm = TRUE),
  West = sum(assignment == "West", na.rm = TRUE),
  East = sum(assignment == "East", na.rm = TRUE),
  n    = n(),   # 👈 add this
  .groups = "drop"
) 

# -------------------------------
# Get centroids for used grid cells
# -------------------------------
grid_centroids <- grid_100km %>%
  filter(grid_id %in% filt_pies$grid_id) %>%
  st_centroid()

# Extract coordinates directly
coords <- st_coordinates(grid_centroids)

grid_centroids <- grid_centroids %>%
  mutate(
    X = coords[,1],
    Y = coords[,2]
  ) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

# Join coordinates to summary
filt_pies <- filt_pies %>%
  left_join(grid_centroids, by = "grid_id") %>% 
  filter(!is.na(X))

# -------------------------------
# Convert coords back to lat/long for plotting
# -------------------------------
filt_pies_sf <- st_as_sf(filt_pies, coords = c("X", "Y"), crs = 5070) %>%
  st_transform(4326)

coords_ll <- st_coordinates(filt_pies_sf)

filt_pies$X <- coords_ll[,1]
filt_pies$Y <- coords_ll[,2]

# -------------------------------
# Define colors
# -------------------------------
pie_colors <- c(
  "Alaska"   = "cyan",
  "West" = "yellow",
  "East" = "#377eb8"
)

# -------------------------------
# Plot
# -------------------------------
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = st_transform(ecoregions_gen, 4326), fill = NA, color = "gray50") +
  geom_scatterpie(
    aes(x = X, y = Y, group = grid_id),
    data = filt_pies,
    cols = c("Alaska", "West", "East"),
    color = NA,
    alpha = 0.9,
    pie_scale = 1
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pie_colors) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(4326)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Wintering Bird Assignments (100 km Grid)")
```

```{r}
# Define all 5 breeding populations and colors
breeding_colors <- c(

  "TX" = "orange",
  "FL" = "purple"
)

# Build the map
ggplot() +
  # Bottom layer: hypso background
  ggspatial::layer_spatial(hypso_bg) +
  # Middle layer: genoscape raster (with transparency)

  # Vector outlines for ecoregions
  geom_sf(data = ecoregions, fill = NA, color = "gray50") +
  # Scatterpie for wintering birds (only actual data)
  geom_scatterpie(

  ) +
  theme_minimal() +

  )
```

#Genoscape with banding and genetic data
```{r}
##banding data
banding_data <- read_delim("input/MigConn/AMKEbandingrecoverymatri")


banding_data <- banding_data %>%
  rename(
    latitude = winter_lat,
    longitude = winter_long
  )

banding_sf <- st_as_sf(
  banding_data,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326
)
banding_sf <- banding_sf %>%
  mutate(
    assignment = Cluster,
    stage_clean = "Banding"
  )
banding_sf$source <- "Banding"


# --- Load data ---
winter_birds <- read_delim("~/genetics_certain1.txt", delim = "\t")

winter_birds <- winter_birds %>%
  mutate(stage_clean = case_when(
    is.na(Stage) ~ "Wintering",
    Stage %in% c("Winter", "Wintering") ~ "Wintering",
    Stage %in% c("Migr", "Migrating") ~ "Migrating",
    TRUE ~ "Wintering"  
  ))

winter_birds <- winter_birds %>%
  rename(
    latitude = Lat,
    longitude = Long
  )

# --- Load ecoregions ---
ecoregion <- st_read("~/Downloads/winter_ecoregion 2/AMKE.winterEcoregions.simple.sf.WGS84.noWater.Ebird.shp") %>%
  mutate(node = case_when(
    Region == "North American Deserts" ~ "NAD",
    Region == "Great Plains" ~ "GP",
    Region == "Eastern Temperate Forests" ~ "ETF",
    Region == "Northwestern Forested Mountains" ~ "NWFM",
    Region == "Marine West Coast Forests" ~ "MWCF",
    Region == "Highland/Interior Mexico" ~ "HIM",
    Region == "Highland Central America" ~ "HCA",
    Region == "Northwest Mexico" ~ "NWM",
    Region == "Atlantic Lowland Mexico" ~ "ALM",
    Region == "California" ~ "CAL",
    Region == "Southcentral US" ~ "SCUS",
    Region == "Southeastern US" ~ "SEUS",
    Region == "Southwest Mexico" ~ "SWM",
    Region == "Northern Andes" ~ "NAndes",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_   
  )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(node))
centroids <- cbind(
  ecoregion,
  st_coordinates(st_centroid(ecoregion))
)

# --- Centroids for labels ---
centroids <- cbind(
  ecoregions,
  st_coordinates(st_centroid(ecoregions))
)

# --- Colors ---
winter_colors <- c(
  "AK" = "cyan",
  "West" = "yellow",
  "East" = "dodgerblue",
  "FL" = "purple", 
  "TX" = "orange"
)
#jitter points
# Convert to sf (WGS84)
winter_sf <- st_as_sf(
  winter_birds,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326
)

# Project to lambert (same CRS you used before)
winter_sf_proj <- st_transform(winter_sf, crs = lamproj)

# Extract coordinates
coords <- st_coordinates(winter_sf_proj)

# Apply jitter (~70 km like your original)
coords[,1] <- coords[,1] + rnorm(nrow(coords), 0, 50000)
coords[,2] <- coords[,2] + rnorm(nrow(coords), 0, 50000)

# Put jittered coords back into sf object
winter_sf_proj$geometry <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(coords),
  coords = c("X", "Y"),
  crs = lamproj
)$geometry

# Transform BACK to WGS84 for raster compatibility
winter_sf_final <- st_transform(winter_sf_proj, 4326)
winter_sf_final$source <- "Genetics"
combined_sf <- bind_rows(winter_sf_final, banding_sf)

# =========================================================
# ️ FINAL MAP
# =========================================================
#to plot alaska on top
ak_points <- winter_sf_final %>% filter(assignment == "AK")
other_points <- winter_sf_final %>% filter(assignment != "AK")

winter_map <- ggplot() +

  # --- Background (same as pie chart map) ---
  ggspatial::layer_spatial(rast("~/winter_background_extended.tif")) +
  ggspatial::layer_spatial(genoscape_rgba, alpha = 1.1) +

  # --- Ecoregions ---
  geom_sf(
    data = ecoregions,
    fill = NA,
    color = "gray50",
    size = 0.2
  ) +

  # --- JITTERED POINTS ---
# Other points first
geom_sf(
  data = combined_sf,
  aes(fill = assignment, shape = stage_clean),  
  color = "black",
  stroke = 0.2,
  size = 2.7,
  alpha = 0.8
) +

# Alaska points LAST (on top)
geom_sf(
  data = ak_points,
  aes(fill = assignment, shape = stage_clean),  
  color = "black",
  stroke = 0.2,   
  size = 2.7,     
  alpha = 0.9
) +
  

  # --- Labels ---
  geom_text(
    data = centroids_filtered,
    aes(x = X, y = Y, label = node),
    size = 3
  ) +

  scale_fill_manual(values = winter_colors) +
  
  scale_shape_manual(
  values = c(
    "Wintering" = 21,  # circle
    "Migrating" = 24, # triangle
    "Banding" = 22 
  ),
  name = "Stage"
)+

  # --- Match pie chart map extent ---
  coord_sf(
    crs = st_crs(4326),
    xlim = c(-160, -60),
    ylim = c(-5, 70),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +

  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.margin = unit(c(0,0,0,0), "cm"),
    legend.position = "right"
  ) +

scale_fill_manual(
  values = winter_colors,
  name = "Breeding Assignment"
) +

guides(
  fill = guide_legend(
    override.aes = list(shape = 21, color = "black")
  ),
  shape = guide_legend(
    override.aes = list(fill = "black", color = "black")
  )
)
# --- Plot ---
winter_map

ggsave("~/Downloads/combinedgenoscape.pdf",
       winter_map,
       width = 10,
       height = 8)
```

# BUILD PIES FROM COMBINED DATA (GENETICS + BANDING)
```{r}

# --- extract coordinates ---
combined_sf <- combined_sf %>%
  mutate(
    X = st_coordinates(.)[,1],
    Y = st_coordinates(.)[,2]
  )

grid <- st_make_grid(combined_sf, cellsize = 1.5)

grid_sf <- st_sf(
  grid_id = 1:length(grid),
  geometry = grid
)

# --- assign to existing grid ---
combined_with_grid <- st_join(combined_sf, grid_sf)

# ---count individuals per cluster per grid ---
pie_data_combined <- combined_with_grid %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(grid_id, assignment) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop")

# --- wide format for scatterpie ---
pie_wide_combined <- pie_data_combined %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = assignment,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )

# --- total count per grid ---
pie_wide_combined <- pie_wide_combined %>%
mutate(
  n = rowSums(across(c(AK, West, East, TX, FL)), na.rm = TRUE)
)

# ---  filter small samples (same rule as before) ---
filt_pies_combined <- pie_wide_combined %>%
  filter(n >= 3)

# --- attach coordinates from your existing grid centroids ---
coords_df <- grid_sf %>%
  st_centroid() %>%
  mutate(
    X = st_coordinates(.)[,1],
    Y = st_coordinates(.)[,2]
  ) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(grid_id, X, Y)

filt_pies_combined <- filt_pies_combined %>%
  left_join(coords_df, by = "grid_id")


#plotting
# ---  Add abbreviations to ecoregions ---
ecoregions <- ecoregions %>%
  mutate(node = case_when(
    Region == "Highland/Interior Mexico" ~ "HIM",
    Region == "Highland Central America" ~ "HCA",
    Region == "Lowland Central America" ~ "LCA",
    Region == "Atlantic Lowland Mexico" ~ "ALM",
    Region == "Northwest Mexico" ~ "NWM",
    Region == "Southwest Mexico" ~ "SWM",
    Region == "Northern Andes" ~ "NAndes",
    Region == "Amazon/Orinoco-Northern Uplands" ~ "AONU",
    Region == "Caribbean" ~ "CAR",
    Region == "California" ~ "CAL",
    Region == "Southcentral US" ~ "SCUS",
    Region == "Southeastern US" ~ "SEUS",
    Region == "Marine West Coast Forests" ~ "MWCF",
    Region == "Northwestern Forested Mountains" ~ "NFM",
    TRUE ~ Region
  ))

# --- Compute centroids for labeling ---
ecoregion_centroids <- cbind(
  ecoregions,
  st_coordinates(st_centroid(ecoregions))
)

filt_pies_north <- filt_pies_combined %>%
  filter(Y >= 10)

filt_pies_south <- filt_pies_combined %>%
  filter(Y < 10)

south_pie <- filt_pies_south %>%
  summarise(
    AK = sum(AK, na.rm = TRUE),
    West = sum(West, na.rm = TRUE),
    East = sum(East, na.rm = TRUE),
    TX = sum(TX, na.rm = TRUE),

    n = AK + West + East + TX + FL,

    Y = 2   #place it slightly above cutoff so it's visible
  )

filt_pies_final <- bind_rows(
  filt_pies_north,
  south_pie
)

# --- Define breeding colors ---
breeding_colors <- c(
  "AK" = "cyan",
  "West" = "yellow",
  "East" = "dodgerblue",
  "TX" = "orange",
  "FL" = "purple"
)

# ---  Build the map ---

  # Bottom layer: hypso background
  ggspatial::layer_spatial(hypso_bg) +
  
  # Genoscape raster

  # Scatterpie for wintering birds
```
